summary: ARES MISSION is an interactive 2D pixel-art space mission simulator designed to train young astronauts aged 7 to 12.   To address the challenge of creating an engaging space mission trainer, players explore different modules of a space station and Martian base, overcoming hands-on technical challenges and real-world space scenarios that put their problem-solving skills to the test.   This project is important because it transforms complex aerospace concepts into an accessible, entertaining game. By simulating authentic astronaut tasks, ARES MISSION fosters critical thinking, logical reasoning, and decision-making in children while inspiring curiosity about how space stations operate and the future of human space exploration.
details:
What is it and how does it work?Ares Mission: Survival (Misión Ares: Supervivencia) is a 2D pixel-art video game designed for children aged 7 to 12. The player steps into the role of a space mission commander, navigating a top-down base with their astronaut across three missions.

Each day, the player must allocate a limited supply of energy across four critical systems:

  • Life Support (air and water).
  • Greenhouse (food).
  • Laboratory (science).
  • Shelter (radiation protection).

No choice comes without a trade-off: energy spent on shielding reduces food production or scientific output. The solar storms striking the base are real events pulled from the NASA DONKI database—using their actual dates and speeds to calculate warning lead times. Notably, the lunar mission culminates in the severe May 2024 solar storm (Kp 9 level), following the exact chronological sequence in which it occurred. At the end of each day, the game explains what the player did well and what can be improved using real scientific facts. Upon completing the adventure, players earn a personalized certificate featuring their name and rank.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Active learning: Teaches real space science without making children feel like they are studying, helping them grasp what space weather is, why radiation threatens astronauts, and how to make decisions with limited resources.
  • Real-world connection: By experiencing authentic events, children realize that what happens in the game actually happened on the Sun, bridging entertainment with real-world science.
  • Free educational access: Aims to provide schools and families—especially in underserved communities—with a free tool to spark interest in science and space exploration. It works seamlessly as a classroom science activity and can be updated as NASA releases new data.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software

  • Game development: Pure HTML5, CSS, and JavaScript, using Canvas 2D for graphics rendering (built from scratch with no game engines or external libraries).
  • Art: Original pixel art created by our team with crisp pixel scaling.
  • Audio and voice: Sound effects synthesized via the Web Audio API and an integrated voice assistant powered by the Web Speech API.
  • Data pipeline: Python scripts used to retrieve and process data from NASA DONKI (solar storms), NASA OSDR (space biology experiments), and RadLab (radiation measurements aboard the International Space Station).
  • Hosting and hardware: Deployed on GitHub and GitHub Pages. Requires no specialized hardware; runs on any computer, tablet, or smartphone with a web browser.

How is the project creative? Rather than being a passive trivia or Q&A game, children learn by making decisions with meaningful consequences. Threats are never arbitrary because real NASA datasets drive the in-game events. Furthermore, instead of merely punishing mistakes, the game explains every setback with a real scientific fact. Alert-light animations, rocket transit sequences between missions, and the final certificate make the experience feel like an authentic space mission.

Key Factors Considered by Our Team

  • Player age: Short texts, simple language, read-aloud voice narration, and intuitive controls (W, A, S, D, and E, plus mouse click and touch support).
  • Scientific accuracy: All datasets are real and properly cited; only damage and energy values were balanced to keep gameplay fun and fair.
  • Accessibility: Runs directly in the browser with no installation required, optimized for low-end devices and slow internet connections.
  • Age-appropriate content: NASA experiments were carefully curated and rewritten to be engaging and understandable for children.
  • Responsible data use: The game explicitly states that it is not an official NASA product, cites every data source, and complies with each platform's terms of use.
